chmmc-2012-winter-individual-01.title: Count paths
chmmc-2012-winter-individual-01.body:
To return to $0$ the robot makes exactly two forward and two backward moves: $\binom42=6$ of the $2^4=16$ equally likely sequences. Probability $\frac6{16}=\frac38$.

**Answer: $\frac38$**

chmmc-2012-winter-individual-03.title: Heptagon angle sum
chmmc-2012-winter-individual-03.body:
Join $A_1A_7$ to get the heptagon $A_1A_2\dots A_7$, with angle sum $900^\circ$. Because $A_1A_2\parallel A_6A_7$, the interior angles at $A_1$ and $A_7$ sum to $180^\circ$. The interior angles at $A_3,A_4,A_5$ are $360-113=247$, $100$ and $360-122=238$ (the figure is reflex at $A_3$ and $A_5$), totalling $585$. So the interior angles at $A_2$ and $A_6$ sum to $900-180-585=135^\circ$, which are exactly $\angle A_1A_2A_3$ and $\angle A_5A_6A_7$.

**Answer: $135$**

chmmc-2012-winter-individual-05.title: Four rooks next to the pawn
chmmc-2012-winter-individual-05.body:
Nine rooks on eight rows force two rooks in some row and two in some column; a row or column can hold two rooks that do not attack each other only if the pawn lies between them, so the pawn's row holds one rook on each side and its column holds one rook on each side. These four rooks can be placed in $2\cdot5\cdot4\cdot3=120$ ways (left arm has $2$ squares, right $5$, upper $4$, lower $3$). They use up the pawn's row and column and two further rows and two further columns, leaving a $5\times5$ array of free rows and columns for the last five rooks, one per row and column: $5!=120$ ways. Total $120\cdot120=14400$.

**Answer: 14400**

chmmc-2012-winter-individual-07.title: Slice by height
chmmc-2012-winter-individual-07.body:
Put $A$ at height $0$ and $B$ at height $7$ on a common axis. At height $z$ the first cone has radius $\frac{4z}7$ and the second $\frac{3(7-z)}7$. They are equal at $z=3$ (radius $\frac{12}7$). The common region has cross-section radius the smaller one: $$V=\pi\int_0^3\Big(\tfrac{4z}7\Big)^2dz+\pi\int_3^7\Big(\tfrac{3(7-z)}7\Big)^2dz=\frac{\pi}{49}(144+192)=\frac{48\pi}7.$$

**Answer: $\frac{48\pi}{7}$**

chmmc-2012-winter-individual-07.title: Two cones
chmmc-2012-winter-individual-07.body:
The surfaces meet in a circle of radius $\frac{12}7$ at distance $3$ from $A$. The intersection is two cones on this common base, with heights $h$ and $7-h$ (here $3$ and $4$), so $V=\frac\pi3\left(\frac{12}7\right)^2\cdot7=\frac{48\pi}7$.

**Answer: $\frac{48\pi}{7}$**

chmmc-2012-winter-individual-08.title: By the first element
chmmc-2012-winter-individual-08.body:
Let the first element be $k$. If $k=6$ there is one visible element, so $k\le5$ and the visible elements are $k$ and $6$. We need the $5-k$ numbers between $k$ and $6$ (i.e. $k+1,\dots,5$) to come after $6$. Among $6$ and these $5-k$ numbers, $6$ is first with probability $\frac1{6-k}$, so $\frac{5!}{6-k}$ of the $5!$ permutations starting with $k$ are good. Summing: $\sum_{k=1}^5\frac{5!}{6-k}=120+60+40+30+24=274$.

**Answer: 274**

chmmc-2012-winter-individual-08.title: Stirling numbers
chmmc-2012-winter-individual-08.body:
The number of permutations of $n$ with exactly $r$ left-to-right maxima is the unsigned Stirling number $c(n,r)$. For $n=6,r=2$: $c(6,2)=274$.

**Answer: 274**

chmmc-2012-winter-individual-09.title: Chinese remainder theorem
chmmc-2012-winter-individual-09.body:
$k\mid f(k)$, so $[f(6)]^5\equiv0\pmod 6$, $[f(10)]^3\equiv0\pmod{10}$, $[f(15)]^2\equiv0\pmod{15}$. By Fermat, mod $5$: $[f(6)]^5\equiv f(6)\equiv f(1)=21\equiv1$, and $[f(10)]^3\equiv0$, $[f(15)]^2\equiv0$, so $S\equiv1\pmod5$. Mod $3$: $[f(10)]^3\equiv f(10)\equiv f(1)\equiv0$, the other two terms are $0\pmod 3$, so $S\equiv0\pmod 3$. Mod $2$: $[f(15)]^2\equiv f(15)\equiv f(1)\equiv1$, other terms even, so $S\equiv1\pmod2$. Hence $S\equiv21\pmod{30}$ (indeed $21\equiv1\ (5)$, $0\ (3)$, $1\ (2)$).

**Answer: 21**

chmmc-2012-winter-individual-10.title: Circumcircle
chmmc-2012-winter-individual-10.body:
$F$ is the circumcenter, and $D$, $E$ are the midpoints of arcs $BC$, $AC$, so $FA=FB=FC=FD=FE=R$. Triangles $ADF$, $BEF$ are isosceles: $\angle DAF=5^\circ$, $\angle EBF=10^\circ$. Let $\angle FBC=\angle FCB=x$, $\angle FCA=\angle FAC=y$, $\angle FAB=\angle FBA=z$. Then $x+y+z=90^\circ$; the bisector at $A$ gives $y+5=z-5$; the bisector at $B$ gives $x+10=z-10$. Solving: $(x,y,z)=(20^\circ,30^\circ,40^\circ)$, so $\angle ABC=x+z=60^\circ$. By the extended law of sines $AC=2R\sin60^\circ$, so $R=\frac{3}{\sqrt3}=\sqrt3=DF$.

**Answer: $\sqrt3$**

chmmc-2012-winter-individual-11.title: Induction
chmmc-2012-winter-individual-11.body:
Claim: $F_{2n}-1$ is a sum $\sum_{i\in S}F_i$ with $S\subseteq\{1,\dots,2n-1\}$ in exactly $n$ ways. For $n=1$: $F_2-1=0$, only $S=\emptyset$. Assume it for $n$ and consider $F_{2n+2}-1$ with $S\subseteq\{1,\dots,2n+1\}$. If $2n+1\in S$, the rest sums to $F_{2n+2}-1-F_{2n+1}=F_{2n}-1$ using indices $\le 2n-1$ (it cannot use $2n$, since $F_{2n}>F_{2n}-1$): $n$ ways. If $2n+1\notin S$, the largest possible sum is $F_1+\dots+F_{2n}=F_{2n+2}-1$, so $S=\{1,\dots,2n\}$: one way. Total $n+1$. For $n=1006$: $1006$.

**Answer: 1006**

chmmc-2012-winter-individual-12.title: Group by $\lfloor\sqrt k\rfloor$
chmmc-2012-winter-individual-12.body:
For $s^2\le k<(s+1)^2$, $\lfloor\sqrt k\rfloor=s$, and $\sum a_k$ over this range counts squares in $[s^6,(s+1)^6)$, i.e. $(s+1)^3-s^3$ squares. So the sum is $\sum_{s=0}^{9}s\left[(s+1)^3-s^3\right]=\sum_{t=1}^9\sum_{s=t}^9[(s+1)^3-s^3]=\sum_{t=1}^9(10^3-t^3)=9000-2025=6975$.

**Answer: 6975**

chmmc-2012-winter-individual-13.title: Third differences
chmmc-2012-winter-individual-13.body:
Let $g(k)=a+kb+\binom k2c+k^2d+2^{k-1}e+k!\,f$; we know $g(1),\dots,g(5)$ and want $g(6)$. The coefficients of $a,b,c,d$ are polynomials in $k$ of degree $\le2$, so $\Delta^3$, i.e. $g(k)-3g(k-1)+3g(k-2)-g(k-3)$, kills them. This gives $g(4)-3g(3)+3g(2)-g(1)=0=e+11f$, $g(5)-3g(4)+3g(3)-g(2)=42=2e+64f$, hence $f=1$, $e=-11$. Then $g(6)-3g(5)+3g(4)-g(3)=g(6)-126=4e+426f=382$, so $g(6)=508$.

**Answer: 508**

chmmc-2012-winter-individual-14.title: Reflect in the plane of centers
chmmc-2012-winter-individual-14.body:
The spheres' centers lie in a plane $P$, and the configuration is symmetric about $P$, so the second tangent plane is the reflection of the $xy$-plane in $P$. Translating to centers $(0,4,4),(4,0,4),(6,6,5)$, the plane through them is $-\frac1{28}x-\frac1{28}y+\frac27z=1$, normal $(-1,-1,8)$. Reflecting the normal $(0,0,1)$ about this direction: $(a,b,c)=(a,a,c)$ with $a^2+b^2+c^2=1$ and $(0,0,1)+(a,b,c)\parallel(-1,-1,8)$, so $\frac{c+1}{8}=-a$. Then $2a^2+(8a+1)^2=1\Rightarrow 66a^2+16a=0$, $a=-\frac8{33}$ (the root $a=0$ is the $xy$-plane), $c=\frac{31}{33}$, so $\frac ca=-\frac{31}8$.

**Answer: $-\frac{31}{8}$**

chmmc-2012-winter-individual-14.title: Direct equations
chmmc-2012-winter-individual-14.body:
For a unit normal $n$ and offset $d$ the plane is tangent to the sphere at $c_i$ with radius $r_i$ (centers on the same side) iff $n\cdot c_i-d=r_i$. Subtracting the equations gives $n\cdot(c_1-c_2)=0$ and $n\cdot(c_1-c_3)=-1$, and with $|n|=1$ the solutions are $n=(0,0,1)$ and $n=\frac1{33}(8,8,-31)$ up to sign, so $\frac ca=-\frac{31}8$.

**Answer: $-\\frac{31}{8}$**

chmmc-2012-winter-individual-15.title: Primitive root
chmmc-2012-winter-individual-15.body:
We need $a$ to be a unit mod $125$, and $125=5^3$ has a primitive root $g$ (of order $100$). Write $a\equiv g^c$ with $1\le c\le100$ (a bijection between units and exponents mod $100$). Then $a^b\equiv1$ iff $100\mid bc$. Count pairs $b,c\in[1,100]$ with $100\mid bc$: by CRT this is $f(4)f(25)$ where $f(p^2)$ counts pairs in $[1,p^2]$ with $p^2\mid bc$: either one of them is $p^2$ ($2p^2-1$ pairs) or both are multiples of $p$ below $p^2$ ($(p-1)^2$ pairs), so $f(p^2)=3p^2-2p$. $f(4)=8$, $f(25)=65$, answer $520$.

**Answer: 520**

chmmc-2012-winter-individual-15.title: Brute force
chmmc-2012-winter-individual-15.body:
Checking $a^b\bmod125$ for all $125\cdot100$ pairs gives $520$ solutions.

**Answer: 520**
